newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FEATURE-Sukarno stirs controversy even in death.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sukarno stirs controversy even in death.

text.p: Indonesia's founding father Sukarno seemingly cannot rest in peace as his legendary charisma still casts a shadow over the country's politics long after his death.

Last year his daughter Megawati Sukarnoputri was ousted as the leader of a minority party at a government-backed congress for fear that her growing popularity could threaten the re-election of President Suharto in 1998.

In April, the government said it would allow a seminar to reassess the role of Sukarno, Indonesia's first president, in a failed 1965 Communist coup, which led to his downfall and brought Suharto to power. The event was later cancelled after fears that it would reveal too many skeletons.
This time, the issue is Sukarno's grave and his dusty remains.
SUKARNO SAID HE WANTED TO BE BURIED IN BOGOR

After Sukarno died in 1970, Suharto ordered him buried in a common graveyard in Blitar, a remote village in East Java, 600 km (375 miles) east of Jakarta, the place of his birth and site of his mother's grave.
The order went against the wishes of his family who wanted him buried at Batutulis district in Bogor, West Java, about 60 km (37.5 miles) south of the capital Jakarta.

Twenty-seven years after his death it is Sukarno's fourth daughter, Sukmawati Sukarnoputri, who has resurrected the issue that the proclaimer of Indonesian independence should be buried in accordance with his own wishes.
"We will keep supporting the plan to move his grave to Bogor because that was his wish," Sukmawati told Reuters in an interview.

"The decision to have him buried in Blitar was made by the present government. But no government is eternal. Who knows, (someday) there will be government officials who can understand the wish of the family and his (Sukarno's) will," she said.

Sukarno, who proclaimed Indonesia's independence from the Dutch on August 17, 1945, died in disgrace in 1970, five years after the abortive coup blamed on the Indonesian Communist Party (PKI) was crushed by the military led by Suharto.
He was put under house arrest in 1966 and Suharto then banned the PKI and decimated its three million strong membership in a series of army-backed pogroms.
Suharto formally became president in 1967 and has been elected six times unopposed.
But renewed debate over the nature of Sukarno's links to the PKI has not affected his popularity in the mainly Moslem nation of more than 200 million people.

Sukarno, known as "Bung Karno" or "Brother Sukarno", came from exile during the Dutch colonial period to lay the foundations for independence during the more than three years of Japanese occupation during the Second World War.

He devised the country's ideology, Pancasila, which welded together Indonesia's hundreds of ethnic groups into a nation under the five principles of belief in one God, humanitarianism, national unity, democracy through consensus and social justice.

A firebrand orator, Sukarno, in an unrivalled political juggling act, led Indonesia first through a five-year war of independence with the Dutch, a failed period of parliamentary democracy, declared martial law and crushed a number of regional separatist movements.
Sukarno retook the former Dutch colony of West Irian, declared he would "crush" the fledgling state of Malaysia, nationalised the economy and threw out foreign companies.

Like a puppet master, Sukarno played off the forces of the military, Islam, nationalism and Communism. The country came to the edge of economic disaster in 1965 when the roller coaster ride came to a crashing end with the coup.

Despite his chequered political record, thousands of people from across the archipelago every year still throng to his grave in Blitar, now enhanced with an elaborate government-funded stone mausoleum.
Shuffling past his glass-encased grave with the reverence of a temple visit they say Moslem prayers and shouts such as "Long Live Sukarno" are common.
SUKARNO'S BURIAL SITE WAS A POLITICAL DECISION
Historian Onghokham said the government's decision to bury Sukarno in Blitar was political because the government is uneasy with the possible revival of so-called Sukarnoism.
Sukarno is a still a popular face for T-shirts and key rings hawked on the streets of the capital and bootleg tapes of his speeches circulate in street markets.
But the government is adamant about its decision not to move Sukarno's grave.
"Let Bung Karno rest in that place peacefully without being disturbed," State Secretary Murdiono said recently.
Sukmawati said: "I believe the decision to put the grave there was in order to make it far away as possible from the centre of power."
